The poet said:
O you who look into this book, ask God for mercy upon its author, and seek forgiveness for its writer.
And seek for yourself the best you desire for it, and after that, forgiveness for its compiler.
The eighth volume of Taysir al-Karim al-Rahman fi Tafsir Kalam al-Malik al-Mannan (Facilitating the Generous One's Mercy in the Exegesis of the Words of the Bountiful King), by its compiler, the one poor in need of God, Abd al-Rahman ibn Nasir ibn Abd Allah, known as Ibn Sa'di, may God forgive him and all Muslims.

It is a Medinan surah.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

This contains good manners (adab) toward God the Exalted and toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the veneration, respect and honour due to him. God commands His believing servants to do what faith in God and His Messenger requires: to carry out God's commands and avoid His prohibitions, to walk behind God's commands, following the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in all their affairs, and not to go ahead of God and His Messenger, so they should not speak until he speaks, and should not give orders until he gives orders. This is the reality of the obligatory adab toward God and His Messenger, and it is the sign of the servant's happiness and success; with its loss, eternal happiness and everlasting bliss are lost. In this there is a strong prohibition against placing the words of anyone other than the Messenger (ﷺ) above his words; for whenever the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) becomes clear, it must be followed and given precedence over anything else, whoever it may be.

{1} Then God commanded taqwa (God-consciousness) in general, which, as Talq ibn Habib said, is: that you act in obedience to God upon a light from God, hoping for the reward of God, and that you abandon disobedience to God upon a light from God, fearing the punishment of God. His saying {Indeed, God is All-Hearing} means: He hears all voices, at all times, in hidden places and directions; {All-Knowing}: of the outward and the inward, the past and the future, and the obligatory, the impossible and the permissible. Mentioning these two noble names after the prohibition against going ahead of God and His Messenger, and after the command of taqwa, urges adherence to those good commands and praiseworthy manners, and warns against their opposite.

{2} Then He, the Exalted, said: {O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another}. This is adab toward the Messenger (ﷺ) in addressing him: the one addressing him should not raise his voice above his voice, nor speak loudly to him, but rather lower the voice and address him with courtesy, gentleness, veneration, honour, reverence and magnification. The Messenger should not be treated as one of them; rather they should distinguish him in their address, just as he is distinguished from others by the obligation of his right upon the community, the obligation to believe in him, and the love without which faith is not complete. For failing to do this carries a danger, and the fear that the servant's deeds may be nullified while he is unaware; just as good manners toward him are among the causes of obtaining reward and having deeds accepted.

{3} Then He praised those who lowered their voices in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), saying that God has tested their hearts for taqwa; that is, tried and examined them, and the result appeared in that their hearts became fit for taqwa. Then He promised them forgiveness for their sins, which includes the removal of evil and harm and the attainment of great reward, whose description none knows except God the Exalted, and in it is the attainment of every beloved thing. In this is evidence that God tests hearts through commands, prohibitions and trials: whoever adheres to God's command, follows His pleasure, hastens to it and prefers it over his own desire, becomes purified and refined for taqwa, and his heart becomes fit for it; and whoever is not like this, it is known that he is not fit for taqwa.

These verses were revealed concerning some of the Bedouin Arabs, whom Allah described as coarse, and who are most deserving of not knowing the limits of what Allah has sent down upon His Messenger. They came as delegations to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and found him in his house and the chambers of his wives. They did not have the patience or good manners to wait until he came out; rather, they called out to him: "O Muhammad, O Muhammad!" meaning: come out to us. So Allah censured them for lacking intellect, since they did not understand from Allah the courtesy and respect due to His Messenger. Indeed, using good manners is part of intellect; the good manners of a servant are a sign of his intellect, and that Allah intends good for him.

Allah says: ﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ That is: He is Forgiving of the sins and breaches of etiquette that proceed from His servants, and Merciful to them, in that He does not hasten to punish them for their sins with penalties and disasters.

{6} This is also one of the etiquettes incumbent upon people of understanding: to adopt and practice it. It is that when a corrupt person (fasiq) brings them a report (naba'), i.e., news (khabar), they should verify his report and not accept it outright, for in that there is great danger and falling into sin. If his report were treated as equivalent to the report of a truthful, upright person, it would be acted upon according to its requirement and implication, and as a result, through that report, souls and wealth would be destroyed without right, which becomes a cause of regret. Rather, the obligation upon hearing the report of a corrupt person is verification and clarification (tabayyun). If indications and circumstantial evidence establish its truthfulness, it is acted upon and accepted; and if they establish its falsehood, it is rejected and not acted upon. In this there is evidence that the report of a truthful person is accepted, the report of a liar is rejected, and the report of a corrupt person is held in suspension. For this reason, the early Muslims (al-salaf) accepted the narrations of many of the Khawarij who were known for truthfulness, even though they were corrupt.

Commentary of Ibn Sa'di (Taysir al-Karim al-Rahman) on surah 49, verses 7–8:

{7} That is: let it be known to you that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is among you. He is the noble Messenger, dutiful and rightly guided, who desires good for you and gives you sincere counsel, while you may want for yourselves evil and harm that the Messenger does not agree with. ﴿Were he to obey you in many matters﴾ it would certainly cause you hardship and distress. But the Messenger guides you, and Allah, exalted is He, makes ﴿faith﴾ beloved to you and beautifies it ﴿in your hearts﴾, by what He has deposited in your hearts of love for the truth and preference for it, by the signs and proofs He has established upon the truth, which indicate its soundness and which hearts and natural dispositions (fitrah) accept, and by His bestowing upon you the guidance to turn to Him. And He makes ﴿disbelief, defiance and disobedience﴾ hateful to you. That is, ﴿defiance﴾ means the major sins, and ﴿disobedience﴾ means the minor sins; by what He has deposited in your hearts of aversion to evil and of not wanting to do it, by the proofs and signs He has established showing its corruption and harmfulness, which natural dispositions do not accept, and by what Allah places in hearts of aversion to it. ﴿Those﴾, that is, those whom Allah has beautified faith for in their hearts, made it beloved to them, and made disbelief, defiance and disobedience hateful to them, ﴿they are the rightly guided﴾; that is, those whose knowledge and deeds are sound, who stand firm upon the upright religion and the straight path. Their opposites are the misguided, for whom disbelief, defiance and disobedience have been made beloved and faith made hateful, and the fault is theirs. When they defied, Allah sealed their hearts; when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate; and when they did not believe in the truth when it first came to them, Allah turned their hearts over.

{8} His saying: ﴿a bounty from Allah and a favor﴾; that is, that good which they attained is by the bounty of Allah upon them and His kindness, not by their own power and strength. ﴿And Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾; that is, He knows who will be grateful for the blessing, so He grants them success in it, and who will not be grateful for it and is not deserving of it, so He places His bounty where His wisdom requires.

{8} His saying: ﴿a bounty from Allah and a favor﴾; that is, that good which they attained is by the bounty of Allah upon them and His kindness, not by their own power and strength. ﴿And Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾; that is, He knows who will be grateful for the blessing, so He grants them success in it, and who will not be grateful for it and is not deserving of it, so He places His bounty where His wisdom requires.

{9} This includes the prohibition for the believers against one of them transgressing against another and some of them killing others. And that when two groups of the believers fight, it is incumbent upon the other believers to rectify this great evil by reconciling between them and mediating in the most complete manner by which reconciliation is achieved, and to take the paths that lead to that. So if the two reconcile, then good, and excellent is that.

{And if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah}; i.e., returns to what Allah and His Messenger have set as limits of doing good and abandoning evil, of which the greatest is fighting.

His saying: {And if it returns, then make peace between them with justice}: this is a command to reconciliation and to justice in reconciliation. For reconciliation may exist while not being with justice, but rather with injustice and wrongdoing towards one of the two disputants. This is not the reconciliation that is commanded. Therefore, neither of them must be favored due to kinship, homeland, or other aims and purposes that would cause deviation from justice.

{Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly}; i.e., those who are just in their judgment among the people, and in all the positions of authority they hold. To the extent that this even includes a man's justice toward his family and dependents in fulfilling their rights. In the authentic hadith: "Those who act justly are with Allah on pulpits of light; those who are just in their judgment, their families, and what they are put in charge of."

{10} {The believers are but brothers}: This is a covenant that Allah established among the believers: that whoever, of any person, anywhere in the east or west of the earth, possesses faith in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, he is a brother to the believers, a brotherhood that requires the believers to love for him what they love for themselves, and to dislike for him what they dislike for themselves. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ), commanding the brotherhood of faith, said: "Do not envy one another, do not inflate prices by bidding against one another, do not hate one another, do not turn away from one another, and be servants of Allah as brothers. The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, nor forsake him, nor lie to him." Agreed upon. And in both (collections) from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The believer to the believer is like a building, one part of it strengthening another," and he (ﷺ) interlaced his fingers between each other.

Allah and His Messenger have commanded the fulfilling of the rights of believers toward one another, and of what achieves affection, love, and connection among them. All of this is a confirmation of their rights over one another. Among that: when fighting occurs between them, which necessitates the division and hatred and aversion of hearts, then the believers must reconcile their brothers, and strive to remove their enmity.

Then He commanded piety in general, and He made mercy the consequence of upholding piety and the rights of the believers, saying: {So that you may receive mercy}. When mercy is obtained, the good of this world and the Hereafter is obtained. This indicates that failing to uphold the rights of the believers is among the greatest barriers to mercy.

Among the benefits of these two verses, other than what has preceded: that fighting between believers is contrary to the brotherhood of faith, and for this reason it is among the greatest of major sins. And that faith and the brotherhood of faith do not vanish with the existence of fighting, just as with other major sins that fall short of shirk; and this is the position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community. And on the obligation of reconciling between believers with justice. And on the obligation of fighting the rebels until they return to the command of Allah, and that if they return in a manner other than the command of Allah, such that they return in a way that is impermissible to acknowledge and adhere to, that is not permitted. And that their property is protected, because Allah permitted their blood only during the duration of their persistence in their rebellion, specifically, and not their property.

And on the obligation of fighting the rebels until they return to the command of Allah, and that if they return in a manner other than the command of Allah, such that they return in a way that is impermissible to acknowledge and adhere to, that is not permitted. And that their property is protected, because Allah permitted their blood only during the duration of their persistence in their rebellion, specifically, and not their property.

{11} This too is among the rights of believers over one another: that "let not a people scoff at a people" by any speech, saying, or deed that indicates belittling a Muslim brother. Such conduct is forbidden and not permissible, and it indicates the mocker's self-admiration, while the one mocked may well be better than the mocker, and this is the usual and actual case. Mockery arises only from a heart filled with bad character traits, adorned with every blameworthy quality and empty of every noble quality. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is enough evil for a person that he belittles his Muslim brother."

Then He said: "And do not defame one another" (lit. do not find fault with yourselves); that is, let not some of you find fault with others. Al-lamz is by speech and al-hamz is by action, and both are prohibited, forbidden, and threatened with the Fire, as Allah the Exalted said: "Woe to every backbiter, slanderer..." (Qur'an 104:1), and the verse continues. He called a Muslim brother "a self" to his brother because believers ought to be in such a state, like one body, and because when someone defames another, he causes the other to defame him in return, so he is the one who brought that about. "And do not insult one another by nicknames": that is, let none of you taunt his brother and give him a nickname he would dislike to be called by. This is tanabuz (mutual insulting by nicknames). As for nicknames that are not disparaging, they do not fall under this. "Wretched is the name of wickedness after faith": that is, how evil is the replacement of faith, and of acting by its laws and what it requires, by the name of wickedness and disobedience, which is insulting one another with nicknames, through turning away from His commands and prohibitions. "And whoever does not repent, then those are the wrongdoers": this is what is obligatory upon the servant: to repent to Allah the Exalted, and to free himself from his Muslim brother's right by seeking his pardon, asking forgiveness for him, and praising him in return for having disparaged him. "And whoever does not repent, those are the wrongdoers": so people are of two kinds: a wrongdoer to himself who does not repent, and a repentant who is successful, and there is no third beyond these.

{12} The Exalted has forbidden much of ill opinion about the believers. {Indeed, some suspicion is sin}: this includes suspicion that is devoid of reality and evidence, and the evil suspicion that is accompanied by many forbidden statements and deeds. For the lingering of evil suspicion in the heart does not confine its holder to mere thought; rather, it continues to drive him until he says what is not fitting and does what is not fitting. Included in this also is thinking ill of a Muslim, hating him, and being hostile to him, whereas he is commanded to do the opposite. {And do not spy}; that is: do not search out the faults of the Muslims, nor pursue them. Leave the Muslim in his condition, and practise overlooking his lapses, which, if they were probed, would reveal what is not fitting. {And let not some of you backbite others}: and backbiting, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your mention of your brother with what he dislikes, even if it is true of him." Then He mentioned a parable to deter from backbiting, saying: {Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it}: He compared eating his flesh when dead, which souls find extremely abhorrent, to backbiting him. Just as you dislike eating his flesh, especially when it is dead and lifeless, so likewise should you dislike backbiting him and eating his flesh while he is alive. {And fear Allah; indeed Allah is Accepting of repentance and Merciful}: At-Tawwab is the One who grants His servant the opportunity to repent, enables him to do so, and then turns to him by accepting his repentance; and Ar-Rahim is merciful to His servants, in that He calls them to what benefits them and accepts their repentance. In this verse is evidence of severe warning against backbiting, and that it is among the major sins, since Allah likened it to eating the flesh of a dead person, and that is among the major sins.

Commentary of Ibn Sa'di (Taysir al-Karim al-Rahman) on surah 49, verse 13:

{13} God, exalted is He, informs that He created the children of Adam from a single origin and a single kind, all of them from male and female, and that they all trace back to Adam and Eve. Yet God scattered from the two of them many men and women, and divided them, and made them ﴿nations (shu'ub) and tribes (qaba'il)﴾; that is, tribes, small and large. This was so that they might come to know one another (ta'aruf). For if each one of them stood alone by himself, that recognition would not have been achieved, and with it would not have arisen mutual support, cooperation, inheritance, and the fulfilment of the rights of relatives. Rather, God made them nations and tribes so that these matters, and others that depend on recognition and the attachment of lineages, might be realised. But nobility lies in piety: the most noble of them in the sight of God is the most pious of them, that is, the one most obedient and most restrained from sins, not the one with the most relatives and kin, nor the one of the most honourable lineage. God is ﴿All-Knowing, All-Aware﴾, knowing among them who stands in the fear of God outwardly and inwardly, and who does not stand in that way either outwardly or inwardly, and He will recompense each according to what he deserves. In this verse there is evidence that knowledge of lineages (ma'rifat al-ansab) is desirable and lawful, because God made them nations and tribes for precisely that purpose.

Commentary of Ibn Sa'di (Taysir al-Karim al-Rahman) on surah 49, verses 14–18:

{14} He (exalted is He) informs about the statement of the Bedouin Arabs (al-A'rab), who entered Islam during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) without insight and without fulfilling what faith requires and entails. Despite this, they claimed and said {We have believed}; that is, complete faith, fully comprehensive of all its matters. This is what the statement necessitates, so Allah commanded His Messenger to respond to them, and He said: {Say, you have not believed}; that is, do not claim for yourselves the station of complete faith, outwardly and inwardly, {but say, "We have submitted"}; that is, we have entered into Islam, and confine yourselves to that. {And} the reason for this is that {faith has not yet entered your hearts}. You only embraced Islam out of fear, or hope, or the like, which are the causes of your faith; therefore the radiance of faith has not entered your hearts. In His saying {and faith has not yet entered your hearts}, it means: at the time of this statement that issued from you. This contains an indication of their condition afterward, for many of them were later blessed by Allah with true faith and jihad in the way of Allah. {And if you obey Allah and His Messenger}: by doing good or abstaining from evil, {He will not deprive you of anything of your deeds}; that is, He will not diminish from them even the weight of an atom, but will repay you in full, in the most complete manner, and you will not lose anything, small or great. {Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful}; that is, Forgiving toward whoever repents to Him and turns back to Him, and Merciful toward him, since He accepts his repentance.

{15} {The believers are only those} who are truly so; that is, {who have believed in Allah and His Messenger and then doubted not and strove with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah}; that is, those who combined faith in Allah and His Messenger with jihad in His way. For whoever fights the disbelievers demonstrates complete faith in his heart, because one who strives against others for Islam, faith, and upholding its laws, then striving against himself for that is all the more fitting and worthy. And whoever is unable to strive is evidence of weak faith. Allah made the absence of doubt (rayb) a condition of faith; that is, the absence of uncertainty, because beneficial faith is the certain conviction in what Allah has commanded belief in, which is not touched by doubt in any way. His saying {Those are the truthful} means: those who affirmed their faith by their good deeds. Truthfulness is a great claim in everything that is claimed, and its holder needs proof and evidence; and the greatest of such claims is the claim of faith, which is the basis of happiness, eternal success, and everlasting salvation. Whoever claims it and fulfills its obligations and requirements is the truthful, true believer. Whoever is not like that is known not to be truthful in his claim, and his claim has no benefit. Faith is in the heart, which none can perceive except Allah the Exalted; so affirming or negating it is a matter of teaching Allah what is in the heart, which is bad manners and an assumption about Allah.

{16} Therefore He said: {Say, "Do you inform Allah of your religion? And Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and Allah is Knowing of all things."} This encompasses all things, among which is what is in the hearts of faith, disbelief, righteousness, and wickedness; He, exalted is He, knows all of that and will recompense for it: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

{17} This is a condition of one who claims faith for himself while not having it. Either this is teaching Allah, while He knows that He is Knowing of all things, or their intention by this statement was to bestow favor upon His Messenger, and that they had given and contributed what was not in their own interests but was rather among his worldly portions. This is adorning oneself with what is not becoming, and boasting about what they should not boast about before His Messenger, for the favor belongs to Allah over them. Just as He is the One who bestows favor upon them with creation, provision, and apparent and hidden blessings, His favor upon them by guiding them to Islam and His favor upon them with faith is greater than everything. Therefore He said: {They consider it a favor to you that they have embraced Islam. Say, "Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has conferred a favor upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful."}

{18} {Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth}; that is, the hidden matters within them that are concealed from creation, such as what is in the depths of the seas, the wastelands of the deserts, and what the night covers or the day conceals. He knows the drops of rain, the grains of sand, the secrets of hearts, and the hidden affairs. {And not a leaf falls but that He knows it, nor is there a grain within the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but that it is in a clear register.} {And Allah is Seeing of what you do}: He counts your deeds for you, repays you in full for them, and recompenses you for them according to what His vast mercy and perfect wisdom require.

The commentary of Surat al-Hujurat is complete by the help, grace, and generosity of Allah. And praise be to Allah.
